public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Hypothesis H

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schinzel%27s_hypothesis_H)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Polynomial
namespace Schinzel

/--
**Schinzel conjecture (H hypothesis)**
If a finite set of polynomials $f_i$ satisfies both Schinzel and Bunyakovsky conditions,
there exist infinitely many natural numbers $n$ such that $f_i(n)$ are primes for all $i$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem schinzel_conjecture (fs : Finset ℤ[X]) (hfs : ∀ f ∈ fs, BunyakovskyCondition f)
    (hfs' : SchinzelCondition fs) : Infinite {n : ℕ | ∀ f ∈ fs, (f.eval (n : ℤ)).natAbs.Prime} := by
  sorry

end Schinzel

reformulations.difference: Wikipedia states Hypothesis H as a disjunction: for nonconstant irreducible integer polynomials with positive leading coefficients, either (1) infinitely many positive integers n make all f_i(n) simultaneously (positive) prime, or (2) some integer m > 1 divides f_1(n)...f_k(n) for every n. The Lean states: `(∀ f ∈ fs, BunyakovskyCondition f) → SchinzelCondition fs → Infinite {n : ℕ | ∀ f ∈ fs, (f.eval n).natAbs.Prime}`. It differs in form in four ways. (i) It is the implication ¬(2) → (1) rather than (1) ∨ (2). (ii) "No fixed divisor" is `SchinzelCondition`: for each prime p there is some n : ℕ with p ∤ f(n) for all f ∈ fs. The source says instead that no integer m > 1 divides the product for all n. (iii) Primality is of `natAbs`, so negative values −p count, and n ranges over ℕ including 0, rather than positive primes at positive integers. (iv) `Irreducible` is taken in ℤ[X], which excludes non-primitive polynomials such as 2X+2, whereas "irreducible over the integers" can be read as irreducible over ℚ.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (i) This is propositional. (ii) Any m > 1 dividing every product has a prime factor p. A prime divides a finite product iff it divides some factor. Polynomial values are p-periodic, since (n − r) ∣ f(n) − f(r). So letting n range over ℕ, positive integers, or ℤ gives the same condition. (iii) Degree ≥ 1 and a positive leading coefficient give f(n) > 0 for all large n, simultaneously for the finitely many f. So the two sets of n differ by a finite set, and `Int.prime_iff_natAbs_prime` applies on the rest. (iv) Under the no-fixed-divisor condition every f is primitive, because a prime dividing the content would be a fixed divisor. By Gauss's lemma (`IsPrimitive.Int.irreducible_iff_irreducible_map_cast`), irreducibility in ℤ[X] and over ℚ then agree. In the ℚ-reading, a non-primitive f makes |content| a fixed divisor, so disjunct (2) holds. Proved in Lean in /workspace/review/equiv.lean. `FileH` is definitionally the theorem's type (`example : FileH := Schinzel.schinzel_conjecture` checks). `WikiH` is the literal Wikipedia disjunction with `Irreducible f` in ℤ[X], positive primes, positive n, and a fixed divisor m > 1 of the product over all n : ℤ. `WikiHQ` is the same with irreducibility over ℚ. The proved results are `file_iff_wiki : FileH ↔ WikiH` and `file_iff_wikiQ : FileH ↔ WikiHQ`, and `#print axioms` shows only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

review.notes: The file has one declaration, `Schinzel.schinzel_conjecture`. I also checked the two shared definitions it relies on, `BunyakovskyCondition` and `SchinzelCondition` (FormalConjecturesForMathlib/Algebra/Polynomial/Basic.lean). Small-case tests in Lean: fs = ∅ gives `Infinite ℕ`, which holds. {X} and the twin-prime set {X, X+2} satisfy both hypotheses. The source's fixed-divisor example {X+4, X+7} provably fails `SchinzelCondition`. So the hypotheses are satisfiable and not vacuous, and they discriminate as intended. The statement is proved equivalent in Lean to a literal transcription of the Wikipedia statement, and also to the reading with irreducibility over ℚ (see reformulations). Status `research open` matches the sources. Wikipedia calls it one of the most famous open problems and says Dirichlet's theorem is the only known case. Skorobogatov–Sofos settle it only for 100% of polynomials. Not formalized, which is fine: Wikipedia's variants (the Schinzel–Sierpiński equivalence with 'at least one n', hypothesis H_N, and integer-valued polynomials, the last flagged 'citation needed'). These are optional additions, not defects. The names 'Bunyakovsky condition' and 'Schinzel condition' do not follow the literature (Skorobogatov–Sofos's 'Bouniakowsky polynomial' means positive leading coefficient plus no fixed prime divisor). The ForMathlib file acknowledges this, and it is a naming matter only. The scan of the 1958 primary source could not be read (image-only PDF, no OCR available). The Wikipedia statement and Skorobogatov–Sofos agree on the formulation.
